books.title: How to Win Friends and Influence People
books.author: Dale Carnegie
books.description: The classic on getting along with people, with advice that still works nearly a century later.
ideas: Don't criticize, condemn or complain
Criticism makes people defensive and rarely changes behaviour. Try to understand why people do what they do instead.
Become genuinely interested in others
You'll make more friends in two months by being interested in other people than in two years trying to get them interested in you.
Remember names
A person's name is, to them, one of the sweetest sounds. Using it shows you see them as an individual.
Talk in terms of their interests
To persuade someone, start from what they care about, not what you want.
Let the other person save face
Even when you're right, a little kindness that lets someone keep their dignity goes a long way.

books.title: Crucial Conversations
books.author: Patterson, Grenny, McMillan & Switzler
books.description: Tools for talking when stakes are high, opinions differ and emotions run strong.
ideas: Start with heart
Before a difficult talk, ask: what do I really want for myself, for them and for the relationship? It keeps you from trying to just win.
Make it safe
When people feel unsafe, they go silent or get aggressive. Restore safety by showing respect and clarifying shared goals.
Separate facts from stories
"You were late three times this week" is a fact. "You don't care" is a story. Lead with facts and offer your story tentatively.
Fill the pool of shared meaning
Good decisions come when everyone's views are on the table. Invite others to share, especially when they disagree.

books.title: Nonviolent Communication
books.author: Marshall B. Rosenberg
books.description: A four-part method for expressing yourself honestly and listening with empathy.
ideas: Observe without judging
Describe what happened like a camera would. "You left dishes in the sink" invites conversation; "You're so lazy" invites a fight.
Express feelings
Say how you feel, using real feeling words: worried, frustrated, relieved. "I feel that you..." is usually a thought, not a feeling.
Connect feelings to needs
Behind every feeling is a need, like rest, respect or connection. Naming the need makes it easier for others to help.
Make clear requests
Ask for a specific, doable action, not a vague demand. "Could you text me if you'll be late?" beats "Be more considerate."

books.title: Never Split the Difference
books.author: Chris Voss
books.description: A former FBI hostage negotiator's techniques for everyday negotiations.
ideas: Tactical empathy
Show the other side that you understand their position and feelings. People negotiate more openly when they feel heard.
Mirroring
Repeat the last few words someone said, as a question. It encourages them to keep talking and reveal more.
Label emotions
Say "It seems like you're frustrated about the timeline." Naming emotions defuses negative ones and builds trust.
Aim for "that's right"
When someone says "That's right" after you summarize their view, they feel understood. That's when real agreement becomes possible.
Calibrated questions
Ask "How am I supposed to do that?" or "What makes this important to you?" Open how and what questions make the other side solve your problem.

books.title: Talk Like TED
books.author: Carmine Gallo
books.description: Lessons from the most popular TED talks on giving presentations people remember.
ideas: Unleash your passion
Audiences connect with speakers who clearly love their subject. Talk about what genuinely excites you.
Tell stories
Stories stick in memory far better than data alone. Wrap your key points in personal, vivid stories.
Keep it to 18 minutes
Long talks overload the brain. Shorter presentations force you to focus on what really matters.
Deliver jaw-dropping moments
Give the audience one surprising, memorable moment, a demo, a shocking statistic, that they'll talk about afterwards.
